Hokm Rules (short starter text).

1) Hokm is usually played by 4 players in teams of two.
2) Each round has a trump suit chosen by the Hakem.
3) Players must follow suit when possible.
4) If a player cannot follow suit, they may play trump or any other card.
5) The team that wins most tricks wins the hand.

Hokm Terms (starter glossary).

Hakem: The player who chooses trump.
Trump (Hokm): The suit that can beat cards from other suits.
Trick: One set of four played cards, one per player.
Lead: The first card played in a trick.
Follow suit: Playing the same suit as the lead card when possible.

History of Hokm.
Hokm is a popular trick-taking card game in Iran and neighboring regions. Its name means "trump" or "ruling suit."
The game likely evolved from older trick-taking traditions and became a social favorite because it is easy to start, strategic to master, and enjoyable in teams.
Over time, families and local groups created small rule variations, but the core idea stayed the same: choose a trump suit, win tricks, and cooperate with your partner.

Hokm Trivia.
• The word "Hokm" refers to the trump suit selected at the beginning of a hand. • Team communication is indirect: players cannot reveal cards, so timing and card memory are important. • Winning early tricks can help read opponents, but holding strong cards for later can also be decisive. • Many players learn Hokm at home, making it both a game and a cultural tradition.

Purpose

Hokm Encyclopedia is an offline reading and learning app about Hokm, also known in some regions as Court Piece or Rang. The content is written by the app team in original explanatory language and is organized for beginners who want a clear path from table setup to strategy. Instead of copying a rule page from the web, the app breaks the game into short lessons, examples, searchable terminology, history notes, and a quiz so users can learn step by step.
Version 1 focus

This release focuses on readable offline lessons, practical examples, a glossary, save/favorite actions, display preferences, and a trivia practice mode. The goal is to provide more value than a quick internet search by combining multiple learning formats in one app: rules, examples, common table variations, cultural context, and review questions. The app does not use copied images, videos, or third-party article text.
Roadmap

Future releases can add diagrams of table position, Persian-language lessons, sample hands, and optional media while preserving fast startup and offline support. When new external references are used, the source list in the app will be updated so users and reviewers can see the origin of factual material.

1. Players and teams 2. Trump and tricks 3. Winning a hand
Players and teams

Hokm is played by four players in two fixed teams of two. Partners sit opposite each other so the turn order alternates between teams around the table. A standard 52-card deck is used and each player eventually receives 13 cards. Many tables deal the first five cards to the Hakem before the trump suit is chosen, then continue dealing the remaining cards in packets. Other tables use packet patterns such as 5-4-4 or 5-5-3. Before play starts, players should agree on the dealing style, target score, penalties for reneging, and whether special results such as winning all tricks receive bonus points.
Trump and tricks

Trump, called Hokm, is chosen at the start of each hand, most often by the Hakem after seeing an initial set of cards. In every trick, the first card sets the lead suit and all players must follow that suit if they can. If a player cannot follow suit, they may play any card: a trump card to try to win the trick or a discard from another suit to protect stronger cards. The highest card in the lead suit wins unless at least one trump is played; when trump appears, the highest trump wins. The winner of each trick leads the next trick, so gaining and keeping the lead is a major strategic advantage.
Winning a hand

A hand contains 13 tricks. Most tables award the hand to the first team that reaches 7 tricks because the other team can no longer catch up. A full game is commonly played to 7 hand points, but families and clubs may choose 5, 9, or another target before starting. Some groups score special outcomes: winning the first seven tricks without allowing the opponents to score can count more, and taking all thirteen tricks can carry a larger bonus. If a player reneges by failing to follow suit while able to do so, the usual friendly-table solution is to correct the trick if discovered immediately or award a penalty hand if discovered later.
1. Hakem 2. Trump 3. Trick and lead
Hakem

Hakem is the player who chooses the trump suit at the beginning of a hand. At many tables the first Hakem is selected by the highest card drawn before the match. After that, the Hakem role usually stays with the winner of the previous hand or passes according to the local rule agreed before play.
Trump (Hokm)

Trump is the ruling suit that can beat cards from other suits when played on a trick. Managing trump means balancing offense and defense: using trump aggressively to capture key tricks, or conserving trump to stop opponent runs later in the hand.
Trick and lead

A trick is one round of four played cards, one card from each player. The lead is the first card in that trick and it decides which suit other players must follow if they hold that suit. The trick winner collects the four cards for their team and leads the next trick.
1. Origins 2. Popularity 3. Local variations
Origins

Hokm developed within the wider family of trick-taking card games, where players follow suit, use a trump suit, and compete to win tricks. In Iran it became known as Hokm because the selected trump suit has a commanding role over other suits. Related games appear under names such as Court Piece or Rang in parts of South Asia, which is why players from different regions often recognize the structure even when local dealing or scoring details differ.
Popularity

Its popularity comes from simple rules, strong strategy depth, and social team-based play. Hokm is often taught informally at home, where people learn practical tactics—counting cards, reading patterns, and coordinating silently with a partner.
Local variations

Families and communities often adopt minor rule variations while the core trump-and-trick structure remains the same. Common differences include who becomes Hakem after a loss, whether dealing is done in 5-4-4 or another packet pattern, how ties are handled near the end of a match, and whether special results such as Beshkan or all-thirteen tricks receive extra value. Because these variations are normal, good etiquette is to explain house rules before the first deal.
1. Name meaning 2. Strategy insight 3. Cultural note
Name meaning

The word Hokm is commonly understood as command, order, or ruling choice. In gameplay it refers to the trump suit, the suit that has special power in each hand. This meaning helps beginners remember that trump cards can override the normal ranking of non-trump suits when players cannot follow the lead suit.
Strategy insight

Top players balance short-term trick wins with long-term control of trump cards and information. They observe small signals such as hesitation, repeated suit leads, and card tempo to estimate likely holdings.
Cultural note

For many people, Hokm is both a game and a shared tradition played across generations. New players often learn by watching relatives, then slowly understand more advanced ideas such as counting suits, protecting partner winners, avoiding unnecessary trump use, and choosing when to sacrifice a low card to gain information.

Origins: Hokm is widely believed to come from Persian trick-taking traditions. The word "Hokm" is commonly understood as "command" or "order," reflecting the authority of the trump suit in each hand.
Spread: Over generations, Hokm became especially popular in Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and among Persian diaspora communities, where it is often played at family gatherings and social events.

Comparison to Court Piece: South Asian Court Piece is very similar in core trick-taking structure and partnership play. However, many Court Piece versions include different bidding or trump-declaration sequences, creating regional tactical differences.
Modern play: Today Hokm is played both in person and online. Mobile apps and web platforms have helped preserve classic rules while introducing the game to younger and global audiences.

Did you know? • In many homes, Hokm is taught informally from older players to younger relatives. • House rules vary by city and family, especially around scoring bonuses. • Digital versions helped diaspora players keep playing together across countries.
